paper_title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.

Introduction Latent recurrent, or looped, language models (LMs) apply shared block of layers repeatedly, so single checkpoint can spend more inference compute per token by running more loops (Dehghani et al., 2019; Geiping et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). When the loop count is varied during training, the same weights can be served at several depths, property we call elastic depth (Geiping et al., 2025; Jeddi et al., 2026). This is an attractive property for model deployment. The loop count enables simple control of quality vs test-time-compute tradeoff, similar to reasoning-effort setting for chain-of-thought, with the difference that no extra tokens are generated. Existing elastic-depth models fall far short of non-recurrent model of equal depth at one loop. For example, Huginn LM, trained with mean recurrence of 32, trails its fixed-depth baseline on nearly every task, scoring 34.9 against 46.4 on ARC-Easy even after 800B tokens (Geiping et al., 2025). Parcae is below its Transformer baseline at one loop and above it at eight (Prairie et al., 2026). We call this gap the one-loop tax. model that pays it must spend several loops recovering ground before additional compute buys anything, so separately trained non-recurrent model remains *Equal contribution. 2026 NVIDIA. The shared recurrent block ℛ𝜃 is applied 𝑘 times between the input ℐ and output 𝒪 blocks. Each loop 𝑖 re-injects ℎin and updates the state with the adaptive-delta rule (Eq. 2), using gate computed from 𝑠𝑖. At 𝑘 = 1, every unique layer executes exactly once. the better choice for the latency-sensitive tier. small loop range does not remove the tax on its own. In our ablations, sampling uniformly over one to five loops still leaves the one-loop endpoint behind the baseline (Section 6.4). Avoiding the tax is different question from whether looping is compute-efficient way to scale model (Prairie et al., 2026; Schwethelm et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026). We take the non-recurrent model as baseline, and ask what it costs to make it elastic without paying the one-loop tax. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), training recipe for looped language models that avoids the tax. ELR partitions backbone into input, shared recurrent, and output blocks, so that at one loop every unique layer executes exactly once and the model has the same parameters and inference compute as non-recurrent model of the same size. Three choices then make the model elastic. The first is the state update. Rather than replacing the state with the recurrent blocks output, ELR takes gated step along the proposed change, with learned step size per token and channel. The second is where loop counts are mixed. Sampling one loop count per optimizer step and varying it across steps, as in Huginns locked-step sampling, does not preserve the one-loop endpoint even when one loop is drawn third of the time. Mixing loop counts within each step does. We implement this by having rotating subset of data-parallel ranks run one loop on every microbatch. The first two choices decide whether the one-loop endpoint survives mixed-depth training. The third is conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget, which lets passes specialize and lowers loss at every added loop. Although recurrent-depth models have been reported to diverge at learning rates that non-recurrent models tolerate (Prairie et al., 2026), every ELR model in this paper trains with its baselines optimizer settings unchanged. The recipe is cheap to apply. Mixed-depth training runs the recurrent block several times per example, but that cost need not be paid over the whole run. Training at one loop for the first three quarters of pretraining and at mixed depth only for the last quarter costs an estimated 16% more training FLOPs than the baseline against 62% for mixed-depth training throughout (for the 4B configuration (Eq. 5)). The conditioning heads are zero-initialized at the switch, so the conditioned model starts as exactly the one-loop checkpoint, and with them the late schedule outperforms mixed-depth training from scratch. For recurrent MoE models, cross-loop route replay evaluates each router once, on the first loop, and reuses its assignments on later loops, cutting mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. During inference, last-loop KV caching keeps single cache that each loop overwrites, so attention KV memory stays at the one-loop level at every loop count. We validate the core of the recipe at two pretraining scales and the full recipe end to end, using 0.5B model to ablate every design choice. We train ELR alongside non-recurrent baselines on the 2 One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models same data at two scales, 4B hybrid model for 1T tokens and 30B-A3B hybrid mixture-of-experts model for 300B tokens. At one loop, ELR is 0.5 points below its baseline on ten-task average at 4B and 1.0 point above it at 30B-A3B. At four loops it is 6.7 and 5.8 points above. Applying the full recipe end to end yields Koi-4B, single checkpoint that scores 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, the level of comparable 4B models, and 29 at four loops, within fixed 4B-parameter footprint. At one loop, ELR reaches similar accuracy to non-recurrent baseline trained on the same data, and every additional loop of the same checkpoint improves it. Elastic depth acquired late in pretraining. Mixed-depth training in the final quarter of the run gives the full loop range for an estimated 16% more training FLOPs than the baseline, and zero-initialized loop conditioning grafted at the switch makes this schedule outperform training at mixed depth from the start. Cross-loop route replay for looped MoE models. Reusing first-loop expert assignments on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% in our experiments with no measurable change in accuracy. Latent Recurrent Models Latent recurrent models, also called looped models, apply shared block of layers repeatedly across depth to iteratively refine hidden state. The idea descends from earlier work on depth-wise weight sharing and adaptive computation (Dehghani et al., 2019; Graves, 2016; Banino et al., 2021), and recent language models adopt it to decouple effective depth from unique parameter count (Geiping et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Bae et al., 2025b). We describe latent recurrent model as composition of three blocks: an input block ℐ with 𝐿in layers, recurrent block ℛ𝜃 with 𝐿rec layers and parameters 𝜃, and an output block 𝒪 with 𝐿out layers. Given token sequence 𝑥, the input block produces fixed representation ℎin = ℐ(Emb(𝑥)), from which recurrent state is initialized and refined by 𝑘 applications of the recurrent block: 𝑠0 = Init(ℎin), 𝑠𝑖 = 𝒢𝜃 (𝑠𝑖1, ℎin), 𝑖 = 1, . . . , 𝑘 The transition map 𝒢𝜃 wraps ℛ𝜃 and specifies how the state is updated at each iteration, with 𝜃 shared across all 𝑘 applications. The output block and language-model head ℋ then map the final state to logits 𝑧 = ℋ(𝒪(𝑠𝑘)). The choices of Init and 𝒢𝜃 vary across architectures: Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025) initializes 𝑠0 from truncated Gaussian and projects the concatenation of 𝑠𝑖1 and ℎin, whereas Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025) has no separate input or output blocks, initializing 𝑠0 from the token embeddings and repeating the full stack without input re-injection. The model has 𝐷unique = 𝐿in + 𝐿rec + 𝐿out distinct layers, but forward pass with loop count 𝑘 traverses 𝐷eff(𝑘) = 𝐿in + 𝑘 𝐿rec + 𝐿out layers, so each additional loop adds 𝐿rec layers of inference compute and latency at fixed parameter count. The loop count may be held constant or sampled from distribution during training. In recurrent MoE model, every loop re-executes the router of each Cross-loop route replay. MoE layer in the recurrent block. Cross-loop route replay instead computes each layers expert assignments and routing weights on the first loop and reuses them on subsequent loops of the same forward pass. The selected experts still process each loops updated representations, so replay removes repeated router evaluation while retaining expert dispatch, communication, computation, and output combination. During training, the load-balancing auxiliary loss is computed once on the first loop and scaled by the realized loop count 𝑘, matching the total weight it receives when accumulated over all 𝑘 loops under dynamic routing. Replay assumes that first-loop routes remain useful at later loops. Section 4.3 tests this assumption by measuring how routing changes across loops and comparing dynamic routing with replay applied at inference only or during training, and reports the resulting training and inference cost. Last-loop KV caching. During inference, latent recurrent models keep one KV cache per loop for each recurrent attention layer. Last-loop KV caching keeps single cache that each loop overwrites, so during decoding, the loop-𝑖 query attends to earlier tokens final-loop keys and values and to the current tokens own loop-𝑖 key and value. Attention KV memory then matches the one-loop model at every 𝑘. Applied at inference to model trained with per-loop caches, the scheme assumes final-loop keys and values remain useful to earlier-loop queries. Section 5.3 shows that the scheme retains the gains from additional loops at close to one-loop cache memory. 4. One-Loop Accuracy and Gains from Additional Loops This section validates the first two choices of the recipe, the adaptive-delta update and within-step mixing with the delayed schedule, against non-recurrent baselines matched in parameters, data, and training horizon. The models here carry no loop conditioning; Section 5 applies the full recipe to post-trained model, and Section 6.6 isolates the effect of conditioning. 4.1. Experimental Setup Models. We evaluate ELR on two hybrid models: GDP-Hybrid-4B, dense model with approximately 4B parameters, and GDP-Hybrid-30B-A3B, mixture-of-experts model with approximately 30B total and 3B active parameters. Both share 52-layer layout of 23 Gated DeltaProduct (GDP) (Siems et al., 2025), 6 self-attention, and 23 feed-forward layers, which are dense MLPs in GDP-Hybrid-4B and MoE layers in GDP-Hybrid-30B-A3B. Each ELR model partitions these layers into 14 input, 24 recurrent, and 14 output layers and is compared with non-recurrent baseline with the same backbone configuration. All ELR models evaluated in this section follow the architecture of Section 3.1 without loop-conditioned modulation. For GDP-Hybrid-30B-A3B, we also train an ELR model with cross-loop route replay (Section 3.4). More details are provided in Appendix A.1. Training. We chose the dense hybrid because it targets the setting where elastic depth matters most. On device with fixed memory budget, 4B model fits where 30B-total mixture of experts does not, and looping lets the model that fits spend compute to close the gap. Last-loop KV inference instead shares one cache across loops. Each loop overwrites the cache, and subsequent tokens read earlier tokens final-loop keys and values. The scheme requires no retraining and keeps attention KV memory at its one-loop size at every 𝑘. The mixed-depth model instead improves monotonically from one to five loops and trades this per-depth optimum for elasticity: single checkpoint serves all five loop counts in place of five separately trained models, at some cost in loss at each depth. The model trained only at 𝑘 = 1 reaches lower loss than the non-recurrent baseline (1.660 versus 1.685), although both execute each unique layer once. Synchronized versus Independent-Rank Loop Sampling The sampling scheme determines how many depths contribute gradients to each optimizer update. Under synchronized sampling, all data-parallel ranks run the same loop count in step, so each update covers one depth, or at most two with one-loop overrides. Under independent-rank sampling, each rank draws its own loop count, so one update can cover every depth, but the step waits for the rank with the largest count. Loss decreases as more depths share an update. One-loop loss falls from 1.6871 under synchronized weighted sampling to 1.6830 with 15% overrides and 1.6774 under independent-rank sampling, and the same ordering holds at every 𝑘 2. Independent-rank sampling gives the lowest loss but increases step time by about 36%. One-loop overrides recover part of this gain at synchronized step time so we use them in our main experiments. 6.4. One-Loop Rank Overrides Under synchronized sampling, one-loop rank overrides are needed for one-loop parity (Figure 5b). Without overrides (𝑓 = 0), uniform sampling reaches one-loop loss +0.0225 above the baseline. Delayed Mixed-Depth Training Delaying mixed-depth training retains most of the gain from additional loops at fraction of its training cost (Figure 5a). Mixed-depth training from scratch costs an estimated 1.79 the baselines training compute (Eq. 5). Starting it after 25%, 50%, or 75% of training tokens lowers this to 1.60, 1.40, and 1.20, while retaining 97%, 90%, and 84% of the five-loop improvement over the baseline. At the 75% start, the estimated added training compute falls from about 79% to 20% for 0.009 increase in five-loop loss, and one-loop loss stays below the baseline at every start point. We therefore use the 75% start for our main experiments (Section 4.1). 6.6. Loop-Conditioned Modulation Loop-conditioned modulation leaves one-loop loss nearly unchanged and lowers loss at every additional loop, with gains growing with loop count (Figure 6). We add the modulation of Section 3.3 to the delayed model that switches to mixed depth after 75% of training tokens, introducing it at the switch with all heads initialized to zero. Loop-conditioned modulation adds 31.6M parameters (6.34% of the GPT-0.5B backbone). One-loop loss moves from 1.6748 to 1.6739, while loss falls by 0.009 at 𝑘 = 2 and by 0.022 at 𝑘 = 5, increasing the loss reduction from one to five loops from 0.038 to 0.059. The conditioned model also achieves lower validation-loss point estimates at every loop count than unconditioned mixed-depth training from scratch (1.6147 versus 1.6273 at five loops), despite using mixed depths only during the final quarter of training. 13 One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models Figure 6 Loop-conditioning on GPT-0.5B. Delayed models switch to mixed depth after 75% of tokens, and the from-scratch model trains at mixed depth throughout. 7. Related Work Elastic recurrent depth. Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025) and Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025) train looped language models whose depth can vary at inference, Mixture-of-Recursions routes tokens to learned recursion depths (Bae et al., 2025b), and LoopFormer conditions shared stack on normalized time and step size so that shortcut trajectories align with the full-depth trajectory (Jeddi et al., 2026). LoopMoE conditions each iteration on its index and the tokens hidden state through an adaptive layer norm (Chen et al., 2026b), and Huginn reports that conditioning the recurrent block on the step index hurt its ability to extrapolate beyond the trained depth (Geiping et al., 2025). Our conditioning uses the same signal as LoopFormer, progress and budget, but is grafted onto trained one-loop checkpoint with zero-initialized heads, so the conditioned model starts as that checkpoint and the deeper passes learn to depart from it; we do not evaluate extrapolation. LoopFormers dense comparisons match either unique parameters or block-level inference FLOPs but not both. During training, Huginn samples single recurrence depth per step, shared by all data-parallel workers (Geiping et al., 2025), whereas the one-loop rank override mixes one-loop and deeper gradients within single update. Closest to our goal, stochastic RINS drops recursion rounds during training and, with depth-specific linear adapters, matches or exceeds training-compute-matched baseline at one recursion in 600M-parameter models (Alabdulmohsin & Zhai, 2025). That result is reported in perplexity, and without the adapters, stronger one-recursion protection reduces gains at higher depths. ELR reaches one-loop parity without depth-specific parameters, with downstream evaluation at 4B dense-hybrid and 30B-A3B MoE scale. Regulating recurrent dynamics. Hyperloop Transformers apply matrix-valued hyper-connections after each loop (Zeitoun et al., 2026), Parcae constrains input-injection dynamics with stability conditions derived from linearized system (Prairie et al., 2026), STARS regularizes the Jacobian spectral radius (Yang et al., 2026), and Training-Free Looped Transformers reinterpret repeated frozen-model computation as damped substeps (Chen et al., 2026a). ELRs adaptive-delta update starts from small step size but learns it end to end without explicit stability constraints, and is designed to match the non-recurrent baseline at one loop while improving with additional loops. Acquiring recurrence late. Retrofitted Recurrence (McLeish et al., 2025) and Relaxed Recursive Transformers (Bae et al., 2025a) convert pretrained non-recurrent models into recurrent ones, using recurrence curriculum and depth-specific low-rank adapters, respectively. Our delayed mixed-depth training instead continues model that is recurrent by construction, changing only the loop-count distribution, with no architectural change or optimizer restart. 14 One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models Recurrent MoE and serving. Sparse Universal Transformer (Tan et al., 2023) and LoopMoE (Chen et al., 2026b) combine sparse expert routing with weight-shared depth. Loopie trains looped MoE models at up to 20B total parameters with fixed two recurrent steps and asks whether looping beats parameter scaling at matched compute (Gao et al., 2026); we instead take the non-recurrent MoE as given and ask what it costs to make it elastic. Read-ME decouples routing from non-recurrent MoE backbone so that expert decisions can be precomputed for scheduling (Cai et al., 2024), whereas cross-loop route replay reuses looped models own first-loop routes on later loops. Continuous Depth Batching schedules tokens that exit at different loop counts (Schwethelm et al., 2026a), whereas we serve each request at fixed loop count. 8. Conclusion Elastic Latent Recurrence shows that looped model can serve single checkpoint across range of inference depths without paying one-loop tax. Three choices make this work. gated adaptivedelta update and within-step mixing of loop counts preserve the one-loop endpoint, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget lets passes specialize, lowering loss at every added loop. At one loop, an ELR model executes every unique layer exactly once; trained on the same data as its non-recurrent baseline, it is 0.5 points below the baseline at 4B and 1.0 point above it at 30B-A3B, and four loops of the same checkpoint add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Elastic depth need not be trained from scratch. Introducing mixed depths in the final quarter of pretraining costs about 1.16 the baselines training compute, and conditioning grafted at the switch with zero-initialized heads makes this late schedule outperform mixed-depth training from the start. Cross-loop route replay cuts mixed-depth update time in recurrent MoE models by 11.7%, and last-loop KV caching holds attention memory at the one-loop level at every depth. Carried through pretraining and post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, single checkpoint that scores 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop and 29 at four loops in our harness. Several questions remain open. Gains diminish after the second loop, which is consistent with later loops appearing in fewer training examples, but we have not tested whether reweighting the loop-count distribution recovers them. Conditioning closes most of the gap to fixed-depth specialists at intermediate depths but not at the endpoints, and we have not isolated why. Our serving setting fixes the loop count per request; combining ELR with per-request or per-token adaptive depth, which budget conditioning complicates, and post-training the MoE variant are the next steps.
